notes.meaning: Judah moved away from his father Jacob and his brothers to live down in the lowlands near Adullam. There he made friends with a Canaanite man named Hirah. Leaving the godly circle of his family to form close friendships with Canaanites placed Judah in spiritual danger.

Judah met and married the daughter of a Canaanite named Shua without consulting his father Jacob. Abraham and Isaac had warned their families against marrying Canaanites, so Judah made an unwise choice driven by his own eyes. Choosing an ungodly spouse often brings sorrow into a home.

Judah and his Canaanite wife had three sons named Er, Onan, and Shelah. Shelah was born at Chezib, a town in the lowlands of Judah. These three boys grew up in a home heavily shaped by Canaanite culture.

Judah arranged a marriage for his firstborn son Er, choosing a woman named Tamar. Arranging marriages was the normal duty of a father at that time. Tamar was brought into Judah's household as the wife of the heir.

Er was extremely wicked in the sight of the Lord, though the Bible does not name his exact misdeeds. God brought sudden judgment upon him and ended his life. God sees all secret sins, and wickedness never escapes his justice.

Judah told his second son Onan to marry Tamar to provide an heir for his dead brother. This ancient practice, known later in the law of Moses as levirate marriage, kept the family name and inheritance alive. It was meant as an act of love and duty toward the deceased brother.

Onan refused to let Tamar have a child because the firstborn would carry his brother's name and share the inheritance. Each time he was with her, he wasted his seed on the ground to prevent a pregnancy. God saw his selfish, hard-hearted disobedience as wicked and put him to death as well.

differ.view: Onan was judged because of his selfish greed and his refusal to fulfill his family duty to raise up an heir for his brother, not because birth control itself is forbidden.
Onan's act of spilling his seed was a severe sin against the natural purpose of marriage and the gift of human life.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: God struck Onan dead because he performed a deliberate contraceptive act that severed marital union from the procreation of life.

notes.meaning: Judah sent Tamar home to live as a widow in her father's house, claiming she should wait until his youngest son Shelah grew up. In secret, Judah feared Shelah would also die if he married her, blaming Tamar instead of his sons' wickedness. Judah unfairly trapped Tamar because custom prevented her from marrying anyone else while pledged to his family.

Years passed, and Judah's wife died. After his time of mourning was finished, Judah and his friend Hirah went up to Timnah for the sheep-shearing season. Sheep-shearing was an annual time of feasting, drinking, and celebration.

Tamar learned that Judah was traveling to Timnah. Realizing that Shelah had grown up and Judah had broken his promise to give him to her, she took off her widow's clothes, covered her face with a veil, and sat along the road at Enaim. She took matters into her own hands through disguise to force an heir from Judah's family.

When Judah passed by and saw her veiled face, he assumed she was a prostitute waiting for customers. Veiling was common for prostitutes in that region and shielded her identity from him. Judah allowed his lust to guide his eyes and mind.
Judah did not recognize his daughter-in-law and asked to sleep with her. Tamar asked what price he would give her. God allowed Judah's senses and moral judgment to be blinded by his desire.

Judah offered to send her a young goat from his flock as payment. Tamar insisted that he leave a security deposit or pledge until the animal arrived. Tamar was not looking for wealth; she wanted personal items she could keep as proof.

Tamar asked for his seal ring, its cord, and the staff in his hand, and Judah agreed and gave them to her. These items served as his personal signature and tribal emblem, identifying him beyond any doubt. Tamar conceived a child through this encounter.

Tamar left right away, removed her veil, and put her widow's garments back on. She returned directly to her quiet life at home. This showed that she had not turned to prostitution as a lifestyle, but used it solely to carry out her plan.

Judah sent his friend Hirah with the young goat to retrieve the personal pledge he had left behind, but Hirah could not find the woman. Judah used a trusted companion so that his shameful behavior would not become public knowledge. Even worldly men often try to hide their sins from others.

Hirah asked the local residents where the shrine prostitute beside the road was, but they replied that no such woman had ever been there. Hirah returned to Judah and reported that he could not find her. The local people knew of no cult prostitute at that location.

Judah decided to drop the search and let the woman keep his items so they would not be publicly laughed at or mocked. He had attempted to honor his bargain with the goat, so he felt content to let the matter rest. Judah cared far more about human embarrassment than about pleasing God.

About three months later, Judah was told that Tamar was pregnant through prostitution. Acting as tribal patriarch, Judah immediately commanded that she be brought out and burned to death for adultery, since she was still bound to Shelah. People are often harsh in condemning sins in others that they secretly practice themselves.

As Tamar was being led out to judgment, she sent Judah's seal, cord, and staff to him with the message that she was pregnant by their owner. She asked him to examine them carefully to see whose they were. Just as Judah had once asked his father Jacob to examine Joseph's coat, Judah was now confronted with his own possessions.

Judah recognized his belongings and confessed that Tamar was more righteous than he was, admitting he had wronged her by withholding his son Shelah. He stopped the punishment and never slept with her again. True repentance includes openly admitting our guilt and turning away from the sin.

When Tamar went into labor, it became clear that she was carrying twin boys. The birth of twins brought both difficulty to the mother and unexpected blessings to Judah's house. God brought new life out of a broken family situation.

During delivery, one baby reached out a hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around his wrist to mark him as the firstborn. The firstborn son had special legal rights and double inheritance in the ancient world. The thread was meant to settle which boy came out first.

The infant pulled his hand back, and his brother burst through and was born first, leading the midwife to cry out over the breach he made. He was named Perez, which means a breach or breaking through. God once again chose the unexpected younger child to hold the preeminent place.

Afterward, the brother with the scarlet thread on his wrist was born and named Zerah, which means rising or brightness. Perez became the ancestor of King David and of Jesus Christ the Savior. God in his great grace used this flawed family to bring about the Redeemer of the world.
